content:
If there's a moment that calls for sense and sensibility in Apple tech, it's yesterday's new iPhone launch.

Having watched yesterday's keynote for the iPhone Duo segment, I was already wiping drool off my desk, but for me, the real star of yesterday's event was the iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max, all because of its new camera features…

Variable aperture – with caveats

Given the supply chain required to bring a variable aperture lens to the iPhone, it's no surprise this feature was thoroughly leaked before launch. The only thing that wasn't entirely clear was whether this would be on both Pro models, or Pro Max only; the good news is the former.

Apple also confirmed that the iPhone will automatically adjust the aperture in some situations, but we can also take full manual control. As I said before, people may need to lower their expectations over how much difference this will make.

However, I also speculated that Apple may have boosted Portrait mode in this latest model, effectively combining the larger aperture with computational photography to produce a result that's better than the hardware alone. This remains to be seen, but looking at some of the sample photos shown, I do suspect I may be right.

I'll be trying it out for myself and, of course, sharing the results.

Low-light photography and video

The maximum aperture is also nearly a stop brighter than the previous generation, jumping from f/1.78 on the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48. While this may not have a significant effect on depth of field, it should be a very useful improvement for low-light shooting, including night shots.

Manual shutter speed control

As well as manual control over aperture, we can also choose shutter speed for stills and video.

For stills, this means we can take long-exposure photos. The promo video demonstrated using this for motion blur effects. We don't yet know what the maximum exposure time will be, nor whether combining the narrowest aperture with computational tricks will allow 30-second exposures – which is what's commonly used to give flowing water that silky look. The same technique can also be used to remove people from a scene.

When using a traditional camera, this would require a neutral density filter to reduce the amount of light coming in, but there are third-party iPhone apps that can combine a series of photos into a single image to achieve a similar effect. I regularly use the Spectre app to shoot in this way.

For video, manual shutter speed control lets us employ the 180-degree shutter rule. Shooting at 24fps, we should set the shutter speed to 1/48 of a second for the most natural-looking motion blur. This was already possible in third-party pro camera apps such as Blackmagic Cam, but it's great news that the built-in Apple app now also has the same feature.

White balance control

White balance control is also a feature that has been available in third-party apps, and it has now made its way into the built-in app.

For stills, this lets us tweak the colour temperature to our personal taste, but it's most important for video footage. With auto white balance, the colour temperature (and thus the whole look of the footage) can drift throughout a clip, giving it an obviously amateur feel. Being able to lock white balance for the duration of a clip is a significant improvement.

Cinematic mode for all video

Cinematic mode is the video version of Portrait mode, letting us apply an artificial shallow depth-of-field effect. Until now, we've had to choose between shooting standard video and Cinematic mode video – although the latter actually also outputs a flat file. The iPhone 18 Pro lets us decide whether to apply the Cinematic mode effect to standard video after the fact.

Furthermore, we can now shoot Cinematic mode video at up to 60fps, making it suitable for slow-motion segments.

Intelligent focus mode for video

Current iPhones already let us set the focus to track a specific person in the frame, but the iPhone 18 Pro introduces a more advanced version.

In particular, it appears to use AI to recognise a specific person and reliably keep tracking them, even if someone walks between us and the subject. Additionally, if the subject leaves the frame and then returns, it can re-acquire the lock.

Histogram

This feature was already reported before yesterday's keynote, so I'll simply repeat what was said at the time.

Battery life

Shooting video drains battery life heavily, so any improvement here is welcome. While we don't yet know the specific figures for shooting purposes, given that the Pro Max's maximum endurance has jumped from 39 hours to 45 hours, this suggests around a 15% increase in shooting time compared to last year's model.

Apple Reference Image

Finally, if you need to prove that a photo is genuine, there's a way to do that. This is clearly a pro tool, best suited to roles such as news photographers and law enforcement.

Wrap-up

Of course, some people will only have eyes for the iPhone Duo, and that's entirely understandable. But if your iPhone is an important part of your camera kit, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the real winners this time around.
